entries.note: Norwegian sea beast meaning a crooked tree or hooked wood; its final -n is the Norwegian definite article, so 'the kraken' repeats 'the', like [[see:La Brea Tar Pits]].
A pleonasm meaning 'the tar tar pits', compared with 'the [[see:kraken]]'.
A historical name for the [[see:kraken]], implying something that grabs.
Another historical name for the [[see:kraken]], suggesting crablike grabbing claws.
Biblical chaos sea serpent with impenetrable scales, from Job, Psalms and Isaiah; a Hebrew word meaning twisted or coiled one, part of the [[see:Chaoskampf]] tradition.
German term for the widespread mythological motif of a hero or god battling a giant chaos monster such as [[see:Leviathan]].
Greek word, possibly just 'snake' in the Iliad, perhaps from a verb meaning to see clearly; came via Latin [[from:draco]] and French into English.
In the Iliad he wears a [[see:dragon]] motif on his sword belt, though it may mean a snake.
Anglo-Saxon predecessor of [[see:dragon]], borrowed directly from Roman Latin before the Normans brought the French word.
A word for a dragon in its own right, related to Latin [[same-root:draco]].
Chinese word for a dragon, thought to echo thunder; used as a suffix in names of dinosaurs found in China, and unrelated to European [[see:dragon]]s.
Old English word for a dragon or serpent, used by Tolkien for [[see:Smaug]]; amusingly reduced to the tiny [[see:earthworm]].
Shows how the mighty [[see:wyrm]] was reduced to a small, fragile serpent.
Tolkien's dragon, described as a [[see:wyrm]] using the Old English term.
Two-legged winged dragon of heraldry, from Old French [[from:guivre]], snake, also javelin; possibly related to [[same-root?:viper]].
Possibly ultimately related to [[same-root?:wyvern]].
Its two-legged winged dragons prompted fans to argue they were really [[see:wyvern]]s.
Its four-legged winged creature counts as a [[see:dragon]] and is never described as a [[see:wyvern]].
Medieval books charting wildlife, mixing real and mythical beasts and giving animals moral qualities; earlier ones existed at Alexandria.
Mythical fire-resistant creature, its name possibly Persian for 'from fire'; the amphibians were named after it, perhaps from crawling out of burning logs.
An amphibian Rob once met, recalled when establishing that real [[see:salamander]]s are amphibians.
Blend of [[from:Elbridge Gerry]] and [[from:salamander]]; his district supposedly looked like a heraldic salamander.
Swaps names with [[see:leopard]] in heraldry, showing the mismatch between heraldic names and appearance, as with [[see:salamander]].
In heraldry a creature that looks like a [[see:lion]] may be called a leopard rampant.
Deadly-gazed king of serpents, from Greek [[from:basilikos]], kingly; literally little king, perhaps after its crownlike crest; tiny in Pliny.
Real lizard that runs on water, named after the mythical [[from:basilisk]].
A kingly word related to [[same-root:basilisk]].
Another kingly word related to [[same-root:basilisk]].
Basilisk-like creature hatched from a cock's egg by a snake, once interchangeable with [[same-root:crocodile]]; thought to come from Latin [[from:calcatrix]], one who tramples.
Formerly interchangeable with [[same-root:cockatrice]]; forms like cockadrill and Latin crocodilus show [[see:metathesis]].
Discussed in an earlier episode.
Half eagle, half horse, meaning horse [[from:griffin]]; surprisingly recent, from [[see:Orlando Furioso]].
Renaissance work in which a knight meets a creature born of a griffin and a mare, the first [[see:hippogriff]].
Named after hooked beaks and claws; first appears in [[see:Aristeas]]'s lost poem; possibly inspired by [[see:Protoceratops]] fossils in the Gobi.
Also named after hookiness, like [[see:griffin]].
Also named after hookiness, like [[see:griffin]].
Semi-legendary Greek poet and miracle worker whose lost poem [[see:Arimaspea]] contains the first known narrative appearance of a [[see:griffin]].
Lost poem by [[see:Aristeas]], surviving in excerpts, about travels in the far north and the [[see:Arimaspi]] battling [[see:griffin]]s.
One-eyed tribe in [[see:Arimaspea]] known for battling gold-guarding [[see:griffin]]s.
Its beaked fossil skulls in the Gobi Desert may have inspired the [[see:griffin]] myth.
Half he-goat, half stag: cervus means stag and hirco- a he-goat; mocked as a boring hybrid, like most antelopes.
Creature in Pliny whose deadly gaze kills, but whose head is so heavy it always hangs to the ground.
Bestiaries claimed these geese emerged from logs or barnacles, so they counted as fish and could be eaten during Lent.
From Old English [[from:mere]], sea, plus maid; compare German [[equivalent:Meerjungfrau]]; often confused with the [[see:siren]].
German for [[equivalent:mermaid]], with Meer, the sea, and specifying a young lady.
Old English term for a water witch or water woman.
Old English word meaning [[see:siren]], whose second element is not 'man'.
Half-bird sea creature often confused with the half-fish [[see:mermaid]]; many languages call mermaids sirens, and depictions are inconsistent.
French word for a [[equivalent:mermaid]], literally [[see:siren]].
Polish word for a [[equivalent:mermaid]], literally [[see:siren]].
French mythical woman, half two-tailed serpent, who left husband [[see:Raymond]] after he broke his promise not to see her on Saturdays, her bath day.
[[see:Melusine]]'s husband, who lost her by seeing her on a Saturday.
Greek mythological woman whose children [[see:Hera]] took away, sometimes said to have been turned into a half serpent.
Overreacting as ever, she took away [[see:Lamia]]'s children.
Reborn-from-ashes bird first appearing in the 8th century BCE; probably 'Phoenician bird' or red bird; Old English fenix was respelled to match [[from?:Phoenician]].
Wise [[see:centaur]] and tutor to heroes like Achilles and Jason, who explains that the [[see:phoenix]] outlives nine ravens.
Greek for bull piercer, perhaps linked to Thessalian mounted hunters; mostly unruly wine-fuelled beings; pronounced differently in Britain and America.
Means one horn, a Latin translation of Greek [[from:monoceros]]; compare German [[equivalent:Einhorn]] and French [[equivalent:licorne]].
German for [[equivalent:unicorn]], literally one horn.
From French unicorne: 'un' was mistaken for the indefinite article and swapped for the definite, a rebracketing like [[see:lingot]].
French for ingot, from l'ingot, another rebracketing like [[see:licorne]].
A rebracketing example discussed in an earlier episode.
A rebracketing example discussed in an earlier episode.
A rebracketing example discussed in an earlier episode.
Greek for one-horned, which gave [[gave:unicorn]]; Pliny's version had a horse's body, deer's head, elephant's feet and a long black horn, rather like a rhino.
Literally nose-horned, sharing the horn element of [[same-root:monoceros]].
Shares the horn element of [[same-root:monoceros]].
Coined in Puerto Rico in 1995, reportedly by [[see:Silverio Pérez]]; Spanish chupacabras is singular, wrongly clipped in English; victims were probably mauled by mangy coyotes.
Newspaper name for the 1975 livestock killer around Moca, Puerto Rico, forerunner of the [[see:chupacabras]].
Used the name [[see:chupacabras]] on San Juan radio in 1995, supposedly while joking about the attacks.
Related to the goat word in [[same-root:chupacabras]]; the shape resembles a goat's hind legs.
Also contains the goat word found in [[same-root:chupacabras]].
Spanish insult meaning big goat, related to [[same-root:chupacabras]].
Rooted in the Greek word for hidden; examples include the [[see:chupacabras]].
The study of hidden animals; Maine has a small cryptozoology museum, and [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] is a key figure.
Belgian zoologist, Nazi-camp escapee and Paris jazz singer, who wrote on unknown animals, including real ones like the [[see:okapi]] and cryptids like [[see:Mokele-mbembe]].
Known locally but doubted by zoologists until seen, as [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] wrote.
Known locally but doubted by zoologists until seen, as [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] wrote.
Known locally but doubted by zoologists until seen, as [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] wrote.
Known locally but doubted by zoologists until seen, as [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]] wrote.
Cryptid of the Congo basin, basically a long-necked sauropod long believed to live there, written about by [[see:Bernard Heuvelmans]].
Younger than [[see:Sasquatch]]; the earliest OED uses refer to real people, such as a Wyandot chief named for his enormous feet.
Older than [[see:Bigfoot]], from a Salish word, originally sasq'ets, translated as hairy mountain men.
From a Sherpa compound variously translated as rocky place plus yellow bear, so roughly rock bear; also called the [[see:abominable snowman]].
Coined by journalist [[see:Henry Newman]] translating [[from:metoh-kangmi]] after [[see:Charles Howard-Bury]]'s Everest expedition; he later admitted it meant more filthy than abominable.
From Latin ab, away, and omen; 1300s–1600s spelling abhominable came from the folk etymology ab homine, away from man.
Sherpa guides' term for whatever made the tracks; kangmi means snowmen, and metoh means filthy or ragged rather than abominable; gave [[gave:abominable snowman]].
British-Irish explorer whose 1920s Everest expedition found big tracks that Sherpas attributed to the [[see:metoh-kangmi]].
Journalist who coined [[see:abominable snowman]] and later apologised for the translation.
Winged, hoofed monster of the Pine Barrens, said to be [[see:Mother Leeds]]'s cursed 13th child; first the [[from:Leeds Devil]], renamed after a 1909 panic.
Original name of the [[see:Jersey Devil]], helped by [[see:Benjamin Franklin]]'s jokes about [[see:Titan Leeds]]'s ghost and a wyvern-like Leeds crest.
Colonial woman who in 1735 cursed her 13th child, which became the [[see:Jersey Devil]].
Place in the Pine Barrens named after the Leeds family, where the [[see:Jersey Devil]] lives.
Almanac printer and rival of [[see:Benjamin Franklin]], who wrote of him as a ghost, feeding the [[see:Leeds Devil]] legend.
Jokingly predicted [[see:Titan Leeds]]'s death in [[see:Poor Richard's Almanack]] in 1733, then wrote of him as a ghost.
[[see:Benjamin Franklin]]'s almanac, where he predicted rival [[see:Titan Leeds]]'s death.
Reported in 1933 by [[see:Alex Campbell]], shortened to [[see:Nessie]] by the 1940s; a 7th-century water beast in the River [[see:Ness]] may be different.
Scottish word for a lake, as in [[see:Loch Ness Monster]].
Scottish Gaelic river name, probably meaning fast-moving water; probably related to Norse [[same-root?:ness]].
Norse word for coastal areas, probably related to the river name [[same-root?:Ness]].
Shortening of [[from:Loch Ness Monster]] in use by the 1940s.
Local water bailiff and part-time journalist who wrote about the [[see:Loch Ness Monster]] in 1933.

entries.translation: Ness dweller with a diamond-shaped fin
entries.note: Scientific name for the [[see:Loch Ness Monster]], coined in 1975 by [[see:Peter Scott]] and [[see:Robert Rines]], possibly as a joke, to classify and protect it.
Naturalist and founder of the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust who coined [[see:Nessiteras rhombopteryx]].
Lawyer and inventor who photographed Nessie's supposed fin and co-proposed [[see:Nessiteras rhombopteryx]].
